About

The Utsunomiya Gyoza Festival is a popular culinary event with stalls run by over 20 gyoza (dumpling) establishments from around the city. The festival began in 1999 to celebrate the gyoza of Utsunomiya with a large number of people, and is held annually on the first Saturday and Sunday of November. A wide variety of gyoza are on offer, including pan-fried, deep-fried, and boiled gyoza. At 100 yen per plate (3 dumplings), a chief attraction of the festival is the opportunity to sample the many options available. Over the two days of this popular event, there will be a variety of activities - including a jazz concert and a talk show - and commemorative stamps will be offered as well.

# Utsunomiya Gyoza Festival

Early November 2026Dates not yet confirmed!

Utsunomiya Castle Ruins Park, Utsunomiya, Tochigi

Utsunomiya is Japan’s “Gyoza Capital,” and the Utsunomiya Gyoza Festival (宇都宮餃子祭り) is the city’s premier culinary celebration. Held annually during the first weekend of November since 1999, the event brings together over 30 leading vendors from the [Utsunomiya Gyoza Association](http://www.gyozakai.com/) at the Utsunomiya Castle Ruins Park. Visitors can sample diverse dumpling styles—fried, steamed, and boiled—at highly discounted prices. The festival features live stage entertainment and mascot appearances, creating a vibrant atmosphere dedicated to the city’s signature soul food. It remains a major destination for culinary tourists seeking authentic regional flavors.

The festival typically operates from 10:00 AM to 4:00 PM over the two-day weekend. Each stall serves a specific variety of gyoza, allowing visitors to compare different wrapper thicknesses and fillings from the city’s most famous specialized restaurants. In addition to the food, the event includes a “Gyoza Sculpture” photo spot and appearances by the city’s mascot, Tsutsumun. Official festival merchandise and frozen gyoza packs are also available for purchase, allowing attendees to take a taste of the festival home.

### Getting there

Utsunomiya is approximately 50 minutes from Tokyo via the JR Tohoku Shinkansen or 100 minutes via the JR Utsunomiya Line. The festival is held at Utsunomiya Castle Ruins Park (Utsunomiya Joshi Koen), located about 15 minutes on foot from the West Exit of Utsunomiya Station. During the festival weekend, dedicated shuttle buses often provide transit between the station and the park to manage the increased volume of visitors. The venue is also accessible via local city buses heading toward the City Hall (Shiyakusho) stop.

Gyoza is renowned as a staple food in Japan, and there are numerous regional variants from all corners of the country. The All Japan Gyoza Festival brings a host of these varieties together in the one spot, with gyoza from popular shops in the Tokai area, to offerings from cities famed for gyoza production such as Utsunomiya in Tochigi, and Hamamatsu in Shizuoka.

There will also be original gyoza available, which will incorporate locally-sourced ingredients from different prefectures.

Getting there

The All Japan Gyoza Festival takes place at Ai-chikyuhaku Kinen Koen (sometimes referred to as Moricoro Park).

**By Public Transport:**

If you're visiting the area via public transport, the closest stop is Ai-Chikyuhaku Kinen Koen Station, on the privately-owned Linimo Line. Due to the large number of visitors expected for the event, public transport is advised.

**By Private Vehicle:**

If you do opt to drive to the venue, there is parking available for 1800 cars, at a cost of 500 yen per vehicle.

web.title: Japan Travel Reports: Utsunomiya, Tochigi Gyoza Festival
web.description: This past weekend in Utsunomiya City, Tochigi Prefecture was the annual Gyoza Festival. Utsunomiya wants to be the Gyoza capital of Japan.
web.markdown:
| | | | --- | --- | | **Travel Reports by scarreddragon** | [view profile of scarreddragon](https://www.japan-guide.com/community/scarreddragon/) | | | | | | --- | --- | --- | | | [list all posts](https://www.japan-guide.com/community/scarreddragon/) | [next post](https://www.japan-guide.com/community/scarreddragon/report-784) | | | | --- | | Note: The opinions and views expressed in this user report are those of the individual author and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and views of japan-guide.com. | #### November 4, 2012 - Utsunomiya, Tochigi Gyoza Festival ![](https://www.japan-guide.com/community/img/675753_4.jpg)Entering the castle grounds and festival This past weekend in Utsunomiya City, Tochigi Prefecture was the annual Gyoza Festival. Utsunomiya wants to be the Gyoza capital of Japan, and there are many gyoza restaurants in Utsunomiya to support that. Many come together at the gyoza festival to offer their specialties for cheap, and as a result the festival is gaining national attention! It seems in previous years the festival was held at Futarasan Shrine mid-way between the JR and Tobu train stations, but this year (perhaps due to size), it was moved to the Utsunomiya castle grounds. ![](https://www.japan-guide.com/community/img/675753_1.jpg)Torii gates at Futarasan We went first to Futarasan shrine, where many Shichi-go-san celebrations were taking place. Because of this, many cute kids were running around in kimono! There were also food stalls set up (none gyoza though), and a live band and other exhibits. ![](https://www.japan-guide.com/community/img/675753_2.jpg)On the stairway of Futarasan Shrine From Futarasan to the castle grounds is a strait walk, about 10-15 minutes. Some parts of the streets were closed with even more food and goods stalls, and even around 10 AM it was getting crowded. ![](https://www.japan-guide.com/community/img/675753_3.jpg) There was a free shuttle bus going to and from the JR station, but the walk wasn't bad either. ![](https://www.japan-guide.com/community/img/675753_5.jpg)Signs showing about how long it will take Already at around 10AM the lines were getting long... these were showing 50 minutes each. We quickly got in somewhat shorter lines, and by the time we got our gyoza (it took about 20-30 minutes), the lines were already at 80 minutes or more. ![](https://www.japan-guide.com/community/img/675753_6.jpg)"Ganbare!" Local junior high school students were on trash duty, and various characters were walking around to take pictures with. There was also a live stage, and lots of free space to sit in the sun or shade around the grounds. ![](https://www.japan-guide.com/community/img/675753_7.jpg)Mmmm, gyoza! Although I was excited to come to Utsunomiya (I love new places!) I didn't really think I'd find the gyoza all THAT good, but actually I was really surprised! These were probably some of the best gyoza I've ever had, and not only was the inside ingredients different and tasty for each type of gyoza, I think the outer dough layer was also really good. It seemed to be a bit thicker than your normal non-Utsunomiya gyoza, which I liked. I can safely say they were worth standing in the 30 minute line for. But 80 minutes? Hmmm... maybe not that good! So If anyone is interested in the festival for next year, I would really recommend it! Utsunomiya is a nice day trip with a few spots for sightseeing but not an overwhelming amount, and the area is really nice this time of year (still a bit early for the fall colors, but shishi-go-san is getting into full swing). If you go, I would recommend making some friends and going in a bigger group, get there right at 10AM or earlier, each of you stand in a different line and get the max amount of orders per person (4 for this year, so 16 gyoza total for 400 yen), meet up, eat, then head around town to explore a bit. When you get hungry later in the afternoon, head back to the festival and do it again. That way you hit the lines when they aren't as bad at the start and miss the lunch rush, then hit the gyoza again right before the close at 3-4PM. The Japanese conception of time is not merely a linear progression of dates, but a complex, polyrhythmic tapestry woven from the lunar calendar, the twenty-four solar terms ( _sekki_), and the ancient agricultural cycle of planting and harvest. This concept is anchored by _matsuri_ (festivals)—events that are not simply religious celebrations, but primary mechanisms for community cohesion. We always recommend including a festival in your trip, a chance for spectacle and to witness locals engaged in ritual and at play. Not to miss are Geisha Matsuri in Kyoto, Tenjin Matsuri in Osaka, or the famed Gion Matsuri, Japan's most famous festival. Also listed below are major art fairs and the annual sumo tournaments, both also peak experiences to consider. The evenings preceding the parades ( **Yoiyama**) turn the streets of Kyoto into a massive open-air party. ## Gion Matsuri Schedule 2026 #### July 10th: Omukae Chōchin (Lantern Reception) At 4:30 PM, men carrying lanterns accompany women and children dressed in elaborate costumes on a procession from Yasaka Shrine along Shijō Street to Kawaramachi Street. These lanterns serve to welcome the portable shrines (mikoshi) when they arrive later at the temporary shrine site. The group pauses in front of Kyoto City Hall to perform traditional music and dance. Later in the evening, they return to Yasaka Shrine to perform again, featuring groups of young girls performing the Sagi Odori (Heron Dance), Komachi Odori (Young Ladies' Dance), and Gion Matsuri Ondo. #### July 10th: Mikoshi Purification Starting at 7:00 PM, the shrine deities are transported from the main hall of Yasaka Shrine to a temporary shrine (otabisho) on the south side of Shijō Street. A large crowd of neighborhood men carries three large and one small mikoshi across the Kamo River. There, Shinto priests purify the shrines in the river water before the bearers continue to their destination. #### July 10th–14th: Hoko-tate, Yama-tate (Float Construction) For the participating neighborhoods, July 10th through the 14th is a time of construction. Residents assemble the massive yama and hoko floats that will be the centerpiece of the upcoming processions. Historically, there were 66 floats—representing the 66 provinces of ancient Japan—but today, roughly 32 floats are built and maintained by local guilds. On the 12th and 13th, "test pulls" are held, allowing the teams to practice maneuvering the massive structures. #### July 13th: Sacred Child Shrine Visit On the 13th, the chigo—a "sacred child" chosen annually from among Kyoto's most prestigious families—visits Yasaka Shrine to pray for the success of the festival. While there are multiple chigo, the most famous is the child seated atop the Naginata-hoko float, who performs the ritual rope-cutting during the main procession. Because the chigo is considered a vessel for the gods during this period, he is carried almost everywhere to ensure his feet do not touch the ground. #### July 14th–16th and July 21st–23rd: Yoiyoiyoiyama, Yoiyoiyama, and Yoiyama For three nights preceding the main parades, locals and visitors flock to the Shijō-Karasuma area to celebrate. These festive evenings are known collectively as Yoiyama. Food stalls line the streets, offering everything from shaved ice to piping hot fried noodles, while the distinct sounds of Gion festival music (Gion-bayashi) echo from all directions. During the Yoiyama period, the floats are illuminated and put on display. Visitors can enter the float headquarters, where historic relics are displayed like miniature museum exhibitions, or purchase lucky charms. In some cases, guests are even permitted to climb inside the floats for a closer look. On the 15th and 16th, traffic is rerouted to turn the area into a pedestrian-only zone. #### July 14th–16th: Byōbu Matsuri (Folding Screen Festival) During these three days, wealthy and influential families in the Shinmachi and Muromachi districts open their doors to the public. This is a rare opportunity to view family treasures accumulated over generations, particularly the magnificent traditional folding screens (byōbu) and other artworks usually hidden from view. #### July 16th: Iwami Kagura Starting at 6:30 PM on the Yasaka Shrine Noh stage, a series of sacred dances is performed by a troupe from Izumo, the birthplace of the Iwami Kagura tradition. The program includes several short classic performances featuring elaborate costumes and masks. Highlights include the story of Shoki the Demon Queller, a battle between heavenly gods, and the legend of the god Susano'o defeating the serpent Orochi. #### July 17th: First Float Procession (Yamaboko Junkō) The climax of the festivities, this procession begins at 9:00 AM and continues along a roughly 2-mile (3 km) route until about 1:00 PM. At Fuyachō Street, the sacred chigo child on the Naginata-hoko float cuts a sacred straw rope, ceremonially marking the start of the parade. Of the festival's roughly 32 floats, two-thirds participate in this first procession. These include the massive hoko (weighing up to 13 tons and standing 80 feet tall) and the smaller yama (weighing 1.5 tons and standing about 20 feet tall). To prevent disputes between neighborhoods regarding the order of the procession, float positions are drawn by lottery. The course begins at Shijō Station, turns north at Kyoto Kawaramachi Station, turns west at Kyoto City Hall, and finishes just past Karasuma Oike. The parade features three massive turns called tsujimawashi—spectacles in their own right, as the wheels do not steer. The sight of colorful, art-draped floats and traditional costumes, combined with the creaking of wooden wheels and festival music, creates the atmosphere of a moving museum. #### July 17th and 24th: Mikoshi Procession On the evenings following the float parades, the portable shrines are taken from their temporary location (otabisho) on Shijō Street to tour the participating neighborhoods, carried on the shoulders of local men. On the day of the first parade (17th), the mikoshi are brought out to the otabisho; on the day of the last parade (24th), they are returned home to Yasaka Shrine. #### July 24th: Second Float Procession (Yamaboko Junkō) The remaining third of the floats participate in this second parade. The course starts from Karasuma Oike station and follows the route of the first parade in reverse, finishing when the floats reach Shijō. #### July 24th: Hanagasa Junkō (Flower Umbrella Procession) Starting at 10:00 AM, ten colorful "umbrella floats" set out from Yasaka Shrine, accompanied by around 1,000 people—mostly women, including Kyoto's famous geiko and maiko (geisha and apprentices). The route crosses the Kamo River and loops past Kyoto City Hall. Various dances are performed along the way, culminating in a final series of dedication dances offered to the gods back at Yasaka Shrine. #### July 30th: Purification at Eki Shrine Closing out the month-long festivities is a summer purification ritual conducted at the Eki sub-shrine within the Yasaka Shrine grounds. Organizers and float guild members gather to receive blessings from a priest and pass through a sacred reed ring (chinowa). Once the dignitaries have finished, the general public is invited to pass through the ring as well to receive a blessing for good health. ![Gion Matsuri procession with float in Kyoto, Japan](https://indochinatravel.com/country/japan/images/1140-gion-matsuri-kyoto%20copy.webp) Procession at Kyoto's famed Gion Matsuri. ### Nachi Fire Festival (Nachi-no-Ogi Matsuri) **July 14, 2026 \| Wakayama** Held at Kumano-Nachi Grand Shrine, this Shinto festival features a dramatic procession of flaming torches and floats through the surrounding cedar forests to the sacred and iconic Nachi Falls. ritual designed to purify 12 deity-carrying portable shrines (Ogi Mikoshi) and their route to the sacred Nachi Falls. Continue to Osaka and check into your final luxury hotel. ## Day 10: Feudal Might & Modern Soul Osaka Castle, a chef-led food tour, and a farewell dinner in Kitahama. Start with a specialized, in-depth tour of the magnificent Osaka Castle, learning about its pivotal role in national unification. Spend the afternoon exploring the dynamic culinary heart of Osaka (Kuromon Market and Dotonbori) with a private chef who can guide you to the city's finest high-end and street-food treasures, explaining the city's unique food philosophy. Conclude with a sophisticated farewell dinner in the trendy Kitahama district before your final night in the city. * * * ##### Tour In Detail ## Japan in full: The New Golden Route Travel between the two cities along the Sea of Japan coast via the New Golden Route. Experience Japan's highlights, though through less-explored and more tranquil and natural parts of the country. Two weeks for your Japan trip provides enough to explore both must-see Tokyo and Kyoto in depth, but also secondary places we recommend and others based on your interests including Osaka, nicknamed "Japan's Kitchen" for its robust food scene. Other recommendations include historic Hiroshima, include Japan's renowned modern "Art Island," Naoshima, the ancient pottery trail through Kyushu, staying at a remote mountain monastery hosted by monks, bucolic Tang Peninsula by e-bike, a ride on one the luxury slow trains that meanders the coast in Kyushu, the many splendors of Ishikawa prefecture, and ancient villages in the Japanese Alps few travelers venture to. Destinations to consider: - **Tokyo** in contrasts, from the neon lit spectacle of Akihabara to the painted faces in Harajuku and the skyscrapers of Shinjuku, to astonishing traditions of sumo. - **Japanese cuisine**, from a serene tea ceremony to famous sushi bars, 12-course kaiseki cuisine to Kobe beef teppanyaki. - Perfectly preserved and wonderfully serene, **Kyoto** is the cultural heartbeat of Japan. There are 17 World Heritage Sites and over 2,000 temples and shrines with a peaceful Buddhist undercurrent. - Ancient treasures fill the massive **Kyushu National Museum**, just one of the attractions in the city of **Fukuoka**, and starting point to explore the ancient pottery trail. - Rituals are all encompassing in Japan. Experience "the way of tea" during a Japanese tea ceremony is a tradition steeped in Zen Buddhism, reflected in slow and graceful movements. Daily, enjoy a soothing **traditional onsen experience** with naturally heated water filling outdoor pools as jagged peaks and pine forests provide the backdrop. - **Cherry blossoms** are the highlight of spring, a captivating bloom blanketing whole cities in two weeks of surreal color. But don't discount the vivid palate of color produced in fall, when profound reds and oranges briefly fill the trees before the leaves cover the pathways. - In **Mount Koya,** delve into Japan's deep Buddhist spirituality, the most formative influence on Japanese history and culture. Included in the potential experiences are tranquil cemetery walks with local nuns and overnighting in a monastery. ![Monks procession on Mount Koya, Japan](https://indochinatravel.com/country/japan/images/700-monk-procession-koyasan-japan.jpg) - **Kanazawa** features well-preserved samurai and geisha districts, but also the country's finest seafood with some of the country's most sublime natural attractions nearby. - Find a different side to Tokyo by spending a morning in the exquisite **Meiji Shrine**, with its beautiful Japanese iris garden enveloping you in tranquility. - Nestled onto forested mountain slopes, the World Heritage villages of **Shirawaka-go and** **Gokayama** are two of Japan's ancient villages. Inaccessible for many centuries and naturally preserved, they're an idyllic getaway from the country's busy cities. - In the far north, **Hokkaido** transforms into a white wonderful during winter. This island of national parks is home to both exhilarating ski slopes and languid cross-country trails, while the capital city Sapporo hosts an annual ice sculpture festival early in February. - In the far southwest, subtropical **Okinawa** features white sands, with swaying palms and jungle-clad retreats found behind the postcard-perfect beaches, as much Hawaiian as it feels like Japan. - **Nara** is home Japan's largest collection of national treasures, including the largest wooden building on Earth and a pair of sublime gardens. * * * ##### Images ![Atomic Bomb dome in Hiroshima](https://indochinatravel.com/country/japan/images/700x520-Hiroshima-Atomic-Bomb-dome.webp) Historic Hiroshima ![Tunnel with cherry blossoms view at the Miho Museum near Kyoto](https://indochinatravel.com/country/japan/images/700x520-miho-museum-tunnel-cherry-blossoms.webp) Miho Museum ![Nijo Castle corner keep](https://indochinatravel.com/country/japan/images/700x520-Nijo-Castle-corner-keep.webp) Nijo Castle * * * [VIEW MORE TRIPS](https://indochinatravel.com/country/japan/japan-tours) [CONTACT US](https://indochinatravel.com/country/japan/japan-festivals#) ![Sushi chef preparing omakase in Tokyo](https://indochinatravel.com/country/japan/images/1024-Musashi-sushi-Aman-Tokyo.webp) **Culinary Japan** Theme **Sushi to Kaiseki** Route **12 Days** Duration **$500 PP/DAY** Starting At ## Sushi to Kaiseki * * * ##### Introduction _Japanese cuisine is not just about the taste, it's also about the beauty and the presentation. The food is_ _a work of art._ —Nobu Matsuhisa From Tokyo, Osaka, and beyond, explore the best of Japan's cuisine—from farm, to market, to table—meeting chefs, mastering dishes, while exploring the country's most spectacular landscapes and sights. Dine where every bite is a sensory delight and every meal a captivating experience. Take in busy food markets, sample sizzling takoyaki and savory yakitori, savor the elegance of Kyoto's multi-course kaiseki, and take a deep dive into the delicate art of sushi, with a private hands-on tuna cutting and sushi making experience with an experienced tuna-cutting master. * * * ##### Highlights - Michelin-starred Ginza omakase and Tsukiji Outer Market tastings - Exclusive sumo stable visit with chanko-nabe lunch - Private ryokan kaiseki banquet in Hakone - Shojin ryori in a Kyoto temple and Nishiki Market tour - Osaka depachika duel, Dotonbori street food, and premium Wagyu farewell * * * ##### Route Map ![Japan culinary adventure route map](https://indochinatravel.com/country/japan/maps/japan-golden-route-new.png) * * * ##### Tour Itinerary ###### Edo, The Shogun’s Seat (Tokyo) Tokyo, the mega-metropolis where centuries-old traditions flourish beneath the neon glow. It is the culinary world's bright star, boasting more Michelin stars than any other city. ## Day 1: Arrival in the Capital Private arrival transfer, landmark hotel check-in, and culinary orientation. Arrival at Tokyo (HND/NRT) and transfer via private luxury car. Check into your landmark hotel (e.g., Aman Tokyo). Welcome cocktail and orientation with your culinary historian guide. ## Day 2: Provenance & Perfection — Tsukiji & Ginza Sushi Tsukiji Outer Market tastings, Ginza architecture, and Michelin omakase. Dawn visit to the iconic Tsukiji Outer Market. Engage with third-generation specialist vendors of everything from dried katsuobushi to premium wasabi, enjoying private tastings with vendors who typically only serve professional chefs. Curator-led tour of the refined Ginza district’s architectural landmarks. In the evening, a pinnacle culinary experience: a private, multi-course omakase dinner at a Michelin-starred Ginza sushi master’s counter, observing the master’s technique up close. ## Day 3: The Dohyo & The Chanko — Exclusive Sumo Access Sumo stable practice, chanko-nabe lunch, Asakusa, and Kappabashi. This morning is dedicated to Grand Sumo. You will have exclusive access to visit a professional Sumo Stable (Asageko). Observe morning practice in silence, witnessing the wrestlers’ rigorous discipline and ritualistic warm-ups. Following practice, enjoy a private lunch with the wrestlers, eating the very food that fuels them: Chanko-nabe, a hearty, protein-rich stew served with sides, prepared by the junior wrestlers. Afternoon dedicated to historic Asakusa, visiting Senso-ji Temple and exploring historic kitchenware street, Kappabashi. ## Day 4: Depachika Delights & Shinjuku Soul Legendary Tokyo food halls and refined Shinjuku izakaya culture. A curator-led tour of a legendary Tokyo Depachika (e.g., Isetan Shinjuku or Takashimaya Ginza). Navigate these high-end food halls to decode the etiquette of luxury fruit gifting, premium Bento box construction, and seasonal wagashi (confections). In the evening, explore Shinjuku’s hidden izakaya culture. While common tourists visit the crowded alleys, you will visit refined, specialist izakayas (e.g., those focused purely on premium Okinawan pork, artisan tofu, or specialized tempura). ###### The Onsen Retreat (Hakone) A vital palate cleanser between the mega-cities. In the forested foothills of Mount Fuji, Hakone is where washoku in its purest form—a ryokan kaiseki—is paired with the restorative ritual of natural onsen. ## Day 5: Shinkansen to Hakone & The Ultimate Ryokan Kaiseki Luxury transfer to Hakone, private onsen ryokan, and in-suite kaiseki. Travel via private vehicle or luxury "Romancecar" train to Hakone. Check into an exclusive luxury ryokan (e.g., Gora Kadan or Hakone Ginyu), featuring private open-air onsen bath with forest or mountain views. In the evening, experience the peak of washoku: a private in-suite Kaiseki banquet. This season-driven meal consists of 10 to 12 courses, each meticulously designed to highlight ingredients at their precise shun (peak moment), served on curated antique ceramics. ###### The Imperial Heart (Kyoto) Kyoto, the capital for over a millennium, is the cradle of traditional Japanese culture. Here, culinary art is entwined with Shinto theology, Buddhist philosophy, and the ritual of the Tea Ceremony. It is the spiritual home of Kaiseki. ## Day 6: Imperial Splendor & Pure Land Gardens Shinkansen to Kyoto, Kinkaku-ji, Ryoan-ji, and an evening in Gion. Travel by Shinkansen to Kyoto. Check into your landmark hotel (e.g., Ritz-Carlton Kyoto). Visit Kinkaku-ji (Golden Pavilion) and the iconic Zen rock garden of Ryoan-ji, decoding the landscape architecture’s connection to Buddhist metaphysics. Evening stroll through the historic Gion district, observing the architecture of the ochayas (teahouses). ## Day 7: The Ritual of Taste — Shojin Ryori & Nishiki Market Nishiki Market tastings, temple shojin ryori, and optional sake brewery. Start with an educational walking tour of Nishiki Market, known as "Kyoto's Kitchen." Sample legendary Kyoto items: yuba (tofu skin), Kyoto pickles (tsukemono), and premium macha. For lunch, experience Shojin Ryori, the sophisticated vegetarian cuisine developed in Buddhist monasteries. Enjoy this minimalist meal in a private temple setting, served by a resident monk. Afternoon free for optional workshops (e.g., artisan sake brewery tour). ## Day 8: Sacred Mountains & Artisan Workshops Private Fushimi Inari access and a curated Kyoto artisan workshop. In the morning, enjoy private, customizable access to the famed red gates of Fushimi Inari Shrine, traveling beyond the main crowds with an expert guide who can explain the Shinto theological connection to agriculture and prosperity. The afternoon is dedicated to a curated artisan workshop (e.g., Kintsugi repair, bamboo weaving, or pottery) at the studio of a distinguished master, gaining unique insight into Kyoto’s enduring craft heritage. ## Day 9: Bamboo Grove & Zen Mindfulness Arashiyama, Tenryu-ji, and a private Geisha and Maiko dinner. Explore the serene Arashiyama district, including the bamboo grove and the Pure Land garden of Tenryu-ji Temple. Enjoy a traditional specialized lunch (perhaps yudofu - hot tofu stew). In the evening, partake in a private, bespoke dining experience with a Geisha and Maiko in a historic teahouse, gaining rare access to this secretive world of traditional performing arts and hospitality. ###### Osaka — The Soul of the Giant and the Spirit of the Rice Osaka is the contrasting mega-city—a vibrant mercantile hub that proudly wears the title "Japan's Kitchen." It is famed for its street food, its dynamic depachikas, distinct culture and personality, and its food philosophy of "Kuidaore" (eat until you drop). ## Day 10: Nara Cradle & Osaka Arrival Todai-ji and Nara Park en route, then Osaka hotel and culinary orientation. Private car to Nara. Visit Todai-ji Temple to view the Great Buddha, learning about the ancient city's deep historical roots. Stroll through Nara Park among the sacred deer. Continue to Osaka and check into your luxury hotel (e.g., St. Regis Osaka). Orientation with your Osaka culinary expert guide. ## Day 11: Depachika Duel & The Soul Food Walk Umeda food halls, Dotonbori classics, and a premium Wagyu farewell. A curated "Depachika Duel". Your guide will navigate you through Osaka’s three massive Umeda food halls (Hanshin, Hankyu, and Daimaru) to experience how Osaka’s mercantile food halls differ from Tokyo’s minimalist refinement—focusing on volume, dynamic displays, and popular "soul foods." In the evening, immerse yourselves in the explosive culinary street culture of Dotonbori. Led by your private guide, sample high-end interpretations of Osaka's classics: gourmet Okonomiyaki, precision-fried Kushikatsu, and high-grade Wagyu Takoyaki. Farewell high-end, premium Japanese Wagyu dinner. ## Day 12: Departure Private transfer to Kansai International Airport. Private luxury transfer from the hotel to Kansai International Airport (KIX). * * * ##### Tour In Detail For many years we've been organizing culinary-first trips in Japan for "food adventurers". From Tokyo all the way to Kanazawa, explore the best of Japan's cuisine, from farm, to market, to table—meeting chefs, mastering dishes, while exploring the country's most spectacular landscapes and sites. Consume not only a cuisine, but a culture and place, where every bite is a sensory delight and every meal a captivating experience. ![Tokyo ramen chef at work](https://indochinatravel.com/country/japan/images/700-ramen-chef-at-work.webp) Take in Tokyo's busy food markets, sampling sizzling takoyaki and savory yakitori, to the tranquil countryside, where traditional tea ceremonies and farm-to-table fare reveal a rich culinary heritage. Delight in the delicate artistry of sushi, with expert chefs transforming the freshest seafood into masterpieces that melt in your mouth. Savor the umami explosion of a steaming bowl of ramen, a comforting symphony of flavors that warms the soul. Be enchanted by the elegance of Kyoto's kaiseki, a multi-course culinary ballet that marks the changing seasons through meticulously prepared dishes. ![Matcha tea serving in Kyoto, Japan](https://indochinatravel.com/country/japan/images/700-japanese-green-tea-cup.webp) During a food-first trip, incredible food is never hard to find in Japan. Learn about the exceptional quality of ingredients, produce, and meats while enjoying the bounty of talented, renowned chefs who are obsessed with crafting their ramen, yakitori, and the world’s finest sushi—in atmospheric settings creating unforgettable dining moments. Explore fish and traditional food markets, legendary sushi bars, busy _izakaya_ (pubs), delicate Zen vegetarian _shojin ryori_ cuisine at a Buddhist monastery, and savory street food in the chaotic alleyways of Osaka. ![Nishiki foods market goods, Kyoto, Japan](https://indochinatravel.com/country/japan/images/700-nishiki-market-goods.webp) Visit Japan's oldest food market, "theaters of food"— _depachika_ food courts—Tokyo’s sprawling “Kitchen Town,” master sushi with a top Tokyo sushi chef, share a traditional yet complex _kaiseki_ dinner with a Geisha in Kyoto, sample street food in Japan's oldest wholesale food mart, sample fresh sake at a top brewery, breakfast with sumo wrestlers in their training stable, and experience a traditional tea ceremony in a sublime garden setting. _"Japan's cuisine? It's like a full-on assault on your taste buds, a gastronomic journey that's as wild_ _and thrilling as a ride down the back alleys of Tokyo on a motorcycle. You think you know sushi? Wait_ _till a master sushi chef in Tsukiji lays down a slice of the freshest tuna that melts in your mouth, a_ _piece so fresh it might have been swimming that morning. Ramen shops in hidden corners, with broths that_ _have been simmering for days, are scenes of reverence. And don't get me started on the street food in_ _Osaka, where every bite is a new adventure, or the traditional Kaiseki dinners that are like 12-act plays_ _on a plate. Wash it down with some local sake, and you're not just eating; you're absorbing a culture, a_ _history, an art form. Japan's food is unapologetic, intricate, and down-right delicious. It doesn't just_ _fill your stomach; it gets under your skin, and good luck shaking it off."_ —Anthony Bourdain * * * ##### Images ![Sushi chef at bar in Tokyo, Japan](https://indochinatravel.com/country/japan/images/700-amamoto-chef-by-City-Foodsters-FlickrCC.webp) Sushi Counter ![Tokyo ramen chef](https://indochinatravel.com/country/japan/images/700-ramen-chef-at-work.webp) Ramen ![Nishiki Market goods in Kyoto](https://indochinatravel.com/country/japan/images/700-nishiki-market-goods.webp) Nishiki Market * * * [VIEW MORE TRIPS](https://indochinatravel.com/country/japan/japan-tours) [CONTACT US](https://indochinatravel.com/country/japan/japan-festivals#) × [Learn More](https://indochinatravel.com/country/japan/japan-festivals#) ×
